title: d4 Sidelines For Black
description: Learn to play against the London, Trompowsky, and other White sidelines after d4 Nf6. Combine with another main course.

lessons.title: White Plays The c3 and e3 Setup

2b1kb1r/1p2pppp/2n2n2/rN1p4/PppP1B2/2P1P.text:
White protects the knight by advancing their a-pawn.

Now we advance our b-pawn one final time, attacking the bishop.

2b1kb1r/1p3ppp/2n1pn2/rN1p4/P1pP1B2/1pP1.text:
And we play ...e6, bolstering d5 and opening up the f8-bishop.

White's position is simply terrible.

We'll proceed by developing our bishops and castling our king.

2r1kb1r/pp2pppp/1q3n2/3p1b2/1n1P1B2/2P2N.text:
But now we jump our knight into the b4-square, exploiting the pin.

Black has a winning advantage.

2r1kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/3p1b2/3P1B2/2P2N2.text: White usually proceeds by developing their other knight.

r1b1kb1r/1p2pppp/1pn2n2/3p4/2pP1B2/2P1P3.text:
White moves their bishop back.

And now we advance our b-pawn.

Our plan is to advance ...b4 (and even ...b3 if allowed) in order to take more space and completely dominate White on the queenside.

r1b1kb1r/1p2pppp/1pn2n2/3p4/2pP1B2/2P1PN.text:
White develops their other knight.

We go ...b5, adding more support to the c4-pawn and taking space.

r1b1kb1r/1p2pppp/2n2n2/1N1p4/1ppP1B2/2P1.text:
White jumps their knight forward, looking to fork our king and rook.

And we'll respond by lifting our rook and attacking White's knight!

If Nc7+ is played now, we can just go ...Kd8 and the knight is stuck.

r1b1kb1r/1p2pppp/2n2n2/1p1p4/2pP1B2/2P1P.text: White develops their light-squared bishop and gets ready to castle.

r1b1kb1r/1p2pppp/2n2n2/1p1p4/2pP1B2/N1P1.text:
The most resilient move for White here is Na3, attacking the b-pawn.

We'll respond by advancing the b-pawn and attacking White's knight.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pp1p/1qn2np1/2pp4/3P1B2/1QP1.text:
White responds by bringing their queen out and offering a trade.

We advance our c-pawn, attacking White's queen and closing in White's light-squared bishop.

We would rather White take.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pp1p/1qn2np1/3p4/2pP1B2/2P1P.text:
White slides their queen back.

Now we develop our light-squared bishop and attack White's queen.

Developing with tempo is important.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/1Qn2n2/3p4/2pP1B2/2P1PN.text:
60% of the time, White trades.

We recapture with our b-pawn.

Our pawns have been doubled, but our rook is well placed on the a-file and we can quickly start advancing  our b-pawn up the board.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/1Qn2n2/3p4/2pP1B2/2PBP3.text:
White is forced to trade queens.

We recapture with the b-pawn.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/2pp4/3P1B2/1PP1P.text:
White's third option is to defend against ...Qxb2 by advancing b3.

This is played 15% of the time.

Against this, we take the d4-pawn.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/2pp4/3P1B2/1PPBP.text:
White's second option is to defend against ...Qxb2 by advancing b3.

This happens 22% of the time.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/2pp4/3P1B2/1QP1P.text:
Most often, White brings their queen out and offers a trade.

This happens 45% of the time.

We'll respond by advancing our c-pawn and attacking the queen.

This pawn push also closes in White's light-squared bishop.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/2pp4/3P1B2/1QPBP.text:
White responds by bringing their queen out and offering a trade.

This is the most common response.

We'll respond by advancing our c-pawn and forking White's pieces.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/2pp4/3P1B2/2P1PN.text:
White can also defend the b-pawn without offering a queen trade, played 20% of the time.

Against Qc2, we'll develop our bishop and attack the queen!

Technically, dxc5 can be played, but few players find that move. 

The idea is that if White naively takes the bishop, we capture the b2-pawn and win White's rook.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/2pp4/3P1B2/2PBP3.text:
White can also defend the b-pawn without offering a trade of queens.

This happens 20% of the time.

Against this, we'll take the d-pawn.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/3p4/2pP1B2/2P1PN.text:
White's other option is to retreat.

Against this, we'll go ...Bf5 and attack White's queen once more!

At first glance, it might seem that the bishop can be captured, but Qxf5 immediately loses to ...Qxb2.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/3p4/3P1B2/1P2PN2.text:
White recaptures with the c-pawn.

We still develop our light-squared bishop to the most active square.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/3p4/3P1B2/1PP2N2.text:
White recaptures with the e-pawn.

Now we develop our light-squared bishop to the most active square.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/3p4/3P1B2/2PB4/P.text:
And when White recaptures...

We can strike in the center!

r1b1kb1r/pp3ppp/1qn2n2/3pP3/5B2/2PB4/PP3.text:
White takes with the d-pawn.

And we respond with ...Ng4. The pawns on f2 and e5 are now under attack.

This ...e5 and ...Ng4 idea exploits the weakness of Qc1: White now doesn't have Qe2 to defend both the pawn on f2 and pawn on e5.

r1b1kb1r/pp3ppp/1qn5/3pP3/5Bn1/2PB3N/PP3.text: White defends f2 with their knight.

r1b1kb1r/pp3ppp/1qn5/3pn3/5B2/2PB3N/PP3P.text:
And we simply grab the e5-pawn.

Black is doing extremely well here. 

White's pieces are misplaced and ...Bxh3 will ruin White's kingside.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pp1p/2n2np1/2pp4/3P1B2/2P1PN.text:
White develops their other knight.

This happens half the time.

We follow up by bringing our queen to b6 and attacking the b2-pawn.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/2pp4/3P1B2/2P1P3/.text:
White's second option is 
the master's approach, played 30% of the time.

Against this, we'll go for ...g6. 

We're trying to play ...Nh5 and fianchetto our bishop, but also generally making a waiting move.

The most natural moves, Bd3 and Ngf3, now run into ...Qb6, and once White goes for the common Qb3-Qc2 maneuver, we've got ...Bf5!

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/2pp4/3P1B2/2P1PN2.text:
White develops the g1-knight.

Roughly 50% of all Londons will end up looking like this.

White allows us an easy plan now.

We'll start by bringing our queen out and attacking the b2-pawn.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/2pp4/3P1B2/2PBP3/.text:
White's third option is to develop their light-squared bishop to d3.

This is played 22% of the time.

Even against Bd3, we'll bring our queen out and attack the b2-pawn.

White can play Qc2 now, but our plan then is simply ...c4 and ...Bf5.

r2qkb1r/5ppp/p1n1pn2/1p1p1b2/P1pP1B2/1PP.text:
We are just in time with ...a6.

Our position is comfortable and we can proceed with ...Be7 and ...O-O.

r2qkb1r/p4ppp/2n1pn2/1p1p1b2/P1pP1B2/1PP.text: And when White tries to undermine further by pushing their a-pawn...

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/3p1b2/2pP1B2/1PP1P.text:
White goes b3, trying to undermine our pawn wedge on the queenside.

We will advance our b-pawn in order to support the c4-pawn.

We are always one step ahead!

r3k2r/pp2bppp/1qn1pn2/3p4/3P1B2/1PPQ1N2/.text:
And we simply develop our bishop.

The position is in the balance, but the engine gives us a slight edge.

We'll castle and bring our rook to the c-file. There are also some ideas to advance the a-pawn.

r3k2r/pp2ppb1/1qn4p/3p1bp1/2pP4/2P1PNP1/.text:
But we can simply play ...Bg7.

We've got the bishop pair, more activity and a space advantage.

We'll castle kingside and should trade if White ever plays b3.

r3kb1r/1p2pppp/2n2n2/1p1p1b2/2pP1B2/2P1P.text:
And we develop our light-squared bishop to the most active square.

Our position is fantastic and we can proceed with ...e6 and ...h6.

r3kb1r/pp2pp1p/1qn2np1/3p1b2/2pP1B2/2P1P.text:
White retreats the queen again.

And now, instead of the ...Qd8 and ...b5 plan, we should go for ...Nh5.

We want to grab White's bishop.

r3kb1r/pp2pp1p/1qn3p1/3p1bBn/2pP4/2P1PN2.text:
White tries to keep their bishop.

We attack the bishop with ...h6.

r3kb1r/pp2pp2/1qn3pp/3p1b1n/2pP3B/2P1PN2.text:
White slides their bishop back.

Now we attack it again with ...g5.

r3kb1r/pp2pp2/1qn4p/3p1bp1/2pP4/2P1PNP1/.text:
White recaptures with the h-pawn.

There is now a threat of Nxg5.

r3kb1r/pp2pp2/1qn4p/3p1bpn/2pP4/2P1PNB1/.text:
White moves the bishop to safety.

We finally capture the bishop.

White's setup allowed us to expand and activate with a lot of tempi moves and eventually remove one of their active pieces.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/2pp1b2/3P1B2/2P1PN.text:
White's other option after ...Bf5 is to slide the queen back a square.

But this is admitting that we outplayed them.

We'll capture the d4-pawn first.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/2pp1b2/3P1B2/2PBPN.text:
White develops their light-squared bishop and interposes the attack.

This is the most common response to ...Bf5, but a pretty big blunder!

We'll capture White's bishop.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/2pp4/3P1B2/2PQPN2/.text:
White recaptures with their queen.

And we take the b2-pawn!

We're going to win White's rook, but our queen is almost trapped and we need to be very careful.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/2pp4/3P1Bb1/1PPBP3.text:
Against this, we'll develop our bishop and attack White's queen.

Our position is quite comfortable.

From here, we have got the simple plan ...e6, ...Be7 and castling, but throwing in ...Nh5 is also possible.

If f3 is played, we can simply go ...Bh5 and bring our bishop to g6.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/3p1b2/2pP1B2/2P1PN.text:
White moves the queen back one square, still guarding the b2-pawn.

Now we play ...e6, bolstering d5 and opening up the f8-bishop.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/3p1b2/3P1B2/1P1BPN.text: And when White offers a trade...

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/3p1b2/3P1B2/1PPB1N.text:
White develops their light-squared bishop, offering a trade of bishops.

We'll respond by trading bishops.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/3p1b2/3P1B2/2P2N2/.text:
White recaptures with the e-pawn.

Recapturing with the c-pawn would have immediately failed to ...Nb4.

Now we bring our rook to the c-file.

The idea is to quickly exploit the placement of the White queen.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/3p4/3P1B2/1PPQ1N2/.text:
White recaptures with the queen.

Now we play ...e6, supporting the d5-pawn and opening our bishop.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/2pp4/3P1B2/2P1PN2/P.text:
White brings their queen back to defend the a2-pawn and prevent our queen from escaping via b2.

The imminent threat is Nbd2, after which we would be forced to give up our queen for the other rook.

We capture the d4-pawn. Now a move like Nbd2 doesn't work since we've got ...Qxc3.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/2pp4/3P1B2/2PQPN2/P.text:
White usually castles their king.

Now we capture the free rook.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/3p4/3P1B2/4PN2/P1Q2.text:
White recaptures with the c-pawn.

We jump our knight into the center.

The point is that Nbd2 now doesn't trap our queen since there's ...Qc3.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/q2p1b2/3P1B2/1P1BPN.text:
We've got the powerful ...Qa5+!

White must now go Kf1 as any other move leads to a loss of material.

Black is much better here.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/2n5/3p4/3PnB2/4P3/P1QN1PP.text:
White brings their knight back with the idea to either trap our queen or trade off our centralized knight.

But the knight has now taken its eyes off the d4-pawn...

So we sacrifice our knight on d4 in order to finally liberate our queen!

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/8/3p4/3PnB2/8/P1QN1PPP/qN.text:
White captures the knight.

We take the pawn with our queen.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/8/3p4/4qB2/8/P1Q2PPP/1N3R.text:
And we recapture with our queen.

Black is completely winning. We're up an exchange and three pawns!

r3kb1r/pp3ppp/1qn1pn2/3p1b2/2pP1B2/2P1PN.text:
White develops their other knight.

Now an important move: we slide the queen back to its home square.

The point is to free up the b-pawn. 

We're anticipating that White might try to undermine our structure.

r3kb1r/pp3ppp/1qn1pn2/3p4/3P1B2/1PPQ1N2/.text: White moves their king to safety.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2pp4/3P1B2/2P1P3/PP.text:
White responds with c3, further supporting their central pawn.

This is the standard London approach for both sides. White getting a dark-squared pawn chain and Black trying to challenge the center.

We'll develop behind our pawn.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/3P1B2/4P3/PPP2.text:
White bolsters their center and opens up the light-squared bishop.

And now we advance our c-pawn, putting pressure on White's center.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/3P1B2/8/PPP1PPPP.text:
White develops their dark-squared bishop to the f4-square, which characterizes the London. 

There are nearly 40 million games in the database from this position. 

It can be reached from multiple move orders, but that shouldn't affect our plan.

Against the London, we should take the center with our d-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to d4 Sidelines for Black!

This course will teach you how to fight against various 1. d4 sidelines.

In this chapter, we'll be taking a look at how to fight the London.

r1b1kb1r/p3p2p/2N2pp1/1qpp4/3P1B2/2P1P3/.text:
We have ...Qb5 to trap the knight.

White now likely has to play Nb8 and get a rook and pawn for two pieces. Black is much better here.

If our queen was on c3, this wouldn't have been possible!

r1b1kb1r/p3p2p/2N2pp1/q1pp4/3P1B2/2P1P3/.text: And if White takes the pawn...

r1b1kb1r/p3pp1p/2p3p1/q1ppN3/3P1B2/2P1P3.text:
White usually jumps their knight forward and attacks the c6-pawn anyway.

This, however, is a mistake! We can simply attack the knight.

r1b1kb1r/p3pppp/2p5/q1pp4/3P1B2/2P1PN2/P.text:
White recaptures.

Now I suggest we go ...g6 and prepare to fianchetto our bishop.

Taking the pawn was possible, but White gets an annoying initiative after a move like Ne5.

r1b1kb1r/p3pppp/2p5/q1pp4/3PnB2/2N1PN2/P.text:
White moves their king to safety.

And we capture the knight.

If White now tries to be tricky by pinning our knight with Qd2, we have ...Ne2+, followed by ...Ba6.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/2B5/q1pp4/3PnB2/2N1PN2/.text:
White usually takes our knight.

We recapture with the c-pawn.

The knight on c3 is still vulnerable.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/qBpp4/3P1B2/2N1PN.text:
White has to go Nc3, blocking the check and defending the bishop.

Now we jump our knight forward and put pressure on the c3-knight.

We're doing to White what they wanted to do to us.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/1Bpp4/3P1B2/4PN2/.text:
White can also develop their light-squared bishop and pin our knight.

This is played 10% of the time.

They want to put pressure on our weak piece and possibly play Ne5 right away.

We respond ...Qa5+ with a double attack on White's king and bishop.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/2pp4/3P1B2/4PN2/P.text:
White develops their other knight.

This isn't very popular, but it's considered to be the best setup.

...Qb6 would now lead to crazy complications, so we'll avoid it.

I suggest we capture the d4-pawn.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/3p4/3P1B2/5N2/PPP.text:
White recaptures with the e-pawn.

And we develop our light-squared bishop to the most active square. 

We want to go ...e6, develop our other bishop and castle kingside.

r2qk2r/pp2bppp/2n1pn2/1B1p1b2/3P1B2/5N2/.text:
We develop our dark-squared bishop and prepare castling.

The position is in the balance.

If Ne5 we can play ...Qb6.

r2qk2r/pp3ppp/2nbpn2/1B1pNb2/3P1B2/2P5/P.text:
Expect White to shove their knight into e5 at this point.

We will just add a defender to the knight.

Nothing to worry about, as White's knight is pinned to the bishop now as well.

r2qk2r/pp3ppp/2nbpn2/3p1b2/3P1B2/2P2N2/P.text:
Against this, we'll also respond ...Bd6 and offer a bishop trade.

Black is comfortable here and we have a handful of plans: castling, ...Qc7, ...Ne4 and even ...Rab8 to start advancing on the queenside.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/1B1p1b2/3P1B2/5N2/.text:
White can also develop their light-squared bishop and pin our knight.

Against this, we should play ...e6 to open up our dark-squared bishop.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/3p1b2/3P1B2/2P2N2/.text:
Roughly 70% of the time, White goes c3, bolstering their center.

Now we play ...e6, preparing to develop our dark-squared bishop.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/1B1p1b2/3P1B2/2P2N.text:
Most often, White develops their other bishop and pins our knight.

Their plan is to go ...Ne5 and put some pressure on the c6-knight.

We'll respond by developing the f8-bishop and offering a trade.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/1B1pNb2/3P1B2/8/PP.text: White jumps their knight forward and puts pressure on our knight.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/3p1b2/3P1B2/2P2N2/.text: White's other option is to develop their light-squared bishop to e2.

r3k2r/ppq2ppp/2nbpn2/1B1pNb2/Q2P1B2/2P5/.text: And if White tries to put even more pressure with a move like Qa4...

r3kb1r/pp3ppp/1qn1pn2/1B1pNb2/3P1B2/8/PP.text:
And we go ...Qb6, supporting our knight and attacking the bishop.

Black is completely fine here.

If a4 we go ...a6, and if c4 we should just capture the pawn.

r4rk1/ppq2ppp/2nbpn2/1B1pNb2/Q2P1B2/2P5/.text:
We can simply castle our king!

The point is that White can't go Nxc6 because of ...Bxf4, and if Bxc6 instead, we play ...bxc6.

Black is doing very well here.

rn1q1rk1/pp2ppbp/5np1/8/2BP1Bb1/2N2N2/PP.text:
And we develop our light-squared bishop to g4, pinning the f3-knight.

Black is doing well here.

Our immediate threat is ...Bxf3 to either ruin White's kingside or win the d4-pawn if White plays Qxf3.

rn1qkb1r/1p1b1ppp/4pn2/2Pp4/1P3B2/4P3/P4.text:
And we play ...Bd7, covering b5 and stopping any Bb5 ideas.

The position is balanced.

We'll go ...b6 and White won't be able to hold onto their extra pawn. 

It's all about the pawn structure here.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/5np1/3p4/2PP1B2/2N2N2/P.text:
White develops their light-squared bishop to e2 and prepares castling.

Now that White has moved the bishop, we capture the c4-pawn.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/5np1/3p4/2PP1B2/2N2N2/PP.text:
White develops their other knight.

We simply castle our king.

Our d5-pawn is still protected and we have easy development ahead.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/4pn2/p1Pp4/1P3B2/2P1P3/P.text:
White supports their b-pawn.

We capture the b4-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/5np1/3p4/2PP1B2/2N5/PP3.text:
White develops the b1-knight.

We fianchetto our dark-squared bishop and get ready to castle.

This is the standard approach against the Panov.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2Pp4/5B2/4P3/PPP2PP.text:
White can also take the c-pawn.

dxc5 only happens roughly 4% of the time, but it is important for us to know how to fight this capture.

We'll respond ...e6, opening up the f8-bishop and threatening to take.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2pp4/2PP1B2/4P3/PP3.text:
White advances their c-pawn only 3% of the time.

They want as much tension in the center as possible.

We respond by taking the d-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2pp4/3P1B2/4PN2/PPP.text:
White's first option is to simply develop their kingside knight.

This happens 21% of the time.

Now we develop our other knight.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/3p4/2PP1B2/8/PP3PPP.text:
White recaptures with the e-pawn.

And now we turn this into a better version of the Panov Caro-Kann with ...g6, preparing to fianchetto.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2Pp4/1P3B2/4P3/P1P2.text:
White advances their b-pawn in order to support to the c5-pawn.

They will probably do this if they choose to capture on c5.

That's why we have to be prepared to undermine the structure immediately.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/3P1B2/4P3/PPP2.text:
White bolsters their center and opens up the light-squared bishop.

We strike at the center with ...c5.

We know what to do if White now bolsters their center with c3, but now there are other options.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/3P1B2/8/PPP1PPPP.text:
White goes for the London by developing their bishop to f4.

Now we take the center with ...d5.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In the second study of this first chapter, we'll cover London setups that don't involve e3 and c3 together.

We will learn how to deal with the Nbd2 setup, and check out some of White's other options move 4.

r1b1k2r/ppp2p1p/2n2p2/3qp3/1b1P4/P1N1P3/.text:
If White attacks it, we have no choice.

We have to remove the knight.

r1b1k2r/ppp2p1p/2n2p2/3qp3/3P4/P1P1P3/5P.text:
The pawn recaptures.

These trades are good for us because we have an active queen and we provoked a weakness from White on the c3-square.

Which we can now attack with ...Qa5.

r1b1kb1r/ppp2p1p/2n2p2/3qp3/3P4/2N1P3/PP.text:
So that they can attack it.

However, chess is not that easy.

We don't have to retreat here and give White the upper hand and d5 opportunities.

We can pin the knight instead and keep our queen in the center.

r1b1kbr1/pp3p1p/1qB2p2/2ppp3/3P4/2P1PN2/.text:
This basically forces a trade.

We'll recapture with the queen and keep our pawn structure intact.

But did we hang a pawn?

r1b1kbr1/pp3p1p/2q2p2/2ppP3/8/2P1PN2/PP3.text: White capturing in the center is no good.

r1bqk2r/pp3p1p/1bn2p2/1B1pp3/8/1NP1P3/PP.text:
Don't be afraid of this pin.

Simply strengthening the center works.

r1bqk2r/pp3p1p/2n2p2/2bpp3/8/1NP1P3/PP3P.text:
White rotates to b3 and attacks our bishop, but we can simply bring it back to b6.

White spent two moves to improve a piece and it doesn't have much potential anyway.

We have a big advantage and it shows.

r1bqkb1r/pp3p1p/2n2p2/1Bppp3/3P4/2P1PN2/.text:
Similar to lines we've covered before, we have a good answer if White pins our knight.

And that's to bring the rook to g8 and attack the g2-pawn.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2p1p/2n2p2/1B1pp3/3P4/4PN2/P.text:
White pins our knight and reintroduces the threat of capturing in the center.

But we've got a strong response against this. The bishop left its post on f1, so we can make use of the g-file and attack the g2-pawn!

White has to make a decision.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2p1p/2n2p2/3Pp3/3P4/4P3/PP3P.text:
It's logical for White to capture on d5.

And bring our queen there.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2p1p/2n2p2/3pp3/2PP4/2N1P3/P.text:
If White brings the knight to c3, we can begin capturing.

On d4 first.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2p1p/2n2p2/8/2pP4/2N5/PP3PPP.text:
And now on c4 as well.

We made these trades to isolate White's d4-pawn and make it weak.

It's already targeted by two pieces.

If White pushes d5, we have ...Qe7+ followed by ...Ne5.

r1bqkbr1/pp3p1p/2n2p2/1Bppp3/3P4/2P1PN2/.text:
White castling could become dangerous.

First, we'll slide the queen to b6 and attack White's bishop.

r2qk1r1/pp3p1p/1bn1bp2/1B1pp3/8/1NP1PN2/.text:
But we can simply continue playing natural moves as we have throughout this line and we are much better.

Moves like ...a6, ...Qd7 and long castling come to mind.

Capturing on c5 rarely pays off for White.

r2qk2r/pp3p1p/1bn1bp2/1B1pp3/8/1NP1PN2/P.text: White will develop the knight at some point.

r2qkbr1/ppp2p1p/2n2p2/1B1pp3/3P2b1/4PN2/.text:
White is already in trouble after ...Bg4.

They won't be able to capture in the center now and ...Qd7 is coming, with what's potentially a strong attack.

We can castle long and develop the dark-squared bishop to d6.

r3k2r/ppp2p1p/2n1bp2/q3p3/3P4/P1P1P3/3Q1.text:
And we can bring the bishop to the natural e6-square.

All of our pieces are active and we have a great position.

We'll castle long and take advantage of the semi-open g-file.

r3kbr1/pp3p1p/2q2p2/2ppP3/8/2P1PN1b/PP3P.text:
After ...Bh3, they are already close to being lost.

The g2-pawn is too vulnerable.

If White plays g3, capturing the rook on f1 is playable, but I advise against it.

Simply ...O-O-O keeps the attack going with a huge advantage.

rnbqk2r/pp3p1p/5p2/2bpp3/8/2P1P3/PP1N1PP.text:
White continues with Nd2, aiming for the b3-square.

We don't have to worry about that yet.

Let's simply continue development.

rnbqkb1r/pp3p1p/5p2/2Ppp3/8/2P1P3/PP3PPP.text:
Capturing on c5 gives up the center completely.

And activates our dark-squared bishop.

rnbqkb1r/pp3p1p/5p2/2ppp3/3P4/2P1PN2/PP3.text:
Our main line will be 6.Nf3, which is played 25% of the time, as mentioned.

There's more pressure in the center, but Black already has an advantage.

We'll defend with the knight.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/5p2/3p4/3P4/4P3/PPP2PP.text:
White traded off their bishop and begins placing pawns on dark squares.

But can't stop our central expansion.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5B2/3p4/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP.text:
White captures on f6 more than 40% of the time, which seems to be the whole point of the opening.

They want to complement the absence of their bishop with pawns on dark squares and force us to play positions without our important kingside knight.

I recommend recapturing with the g-pawn! The idea is simple: ...e5 is coming.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2p1p/5p2/3pp3/2PP4/4P3/PP3PP.text:
White can opt for the active 5.c4 with more tension in the center, which you will face almost as often as 5.c3.

It might seem tempting to play ...c6 and provide reinforcement, but we need the c6-square for the knight.

Our d5-pawn is defended anyway and it's more important to develop and put pressure on the center ourselves.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2p1p/5p2/3pp3/3P4/2P1P3/PP3P.text:
White supports the center just over 20% of the time. It's definitely a solid but more passive route than 5.c4.

Let's try to exploit it by responding actively and create total chaos in the center.

White's structure is under attack from both the e5- and the c5-pawns.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2p1p/5p2/3pp3/3P4/4PN2/PPP2P.text:
White brings the knight out 15% of the time.

It seems unorthodox to allow ...e4 like this and make the knight a target, but that is exactly what White wants.

Pushing ...e4 would commit our pawns to d5 and e4 and leave our f-pawns doubled and meaningless.

Let's defend the center instead, since it was under attack.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/6B1/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP.text:
And here comes the Trompowsky, played 4% of the time and in almost 10 million games.

Most often, the idea is to simply remove our knight from f6 and never worry about the bishop again, which we'll cover in Study 1.

Going for ...d5 works almost every time. We simply contest the center and await White's next move.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
As we already know, the dark-squared bishop can become a problem for White in 1.d4 positions if they have to play e3 before developing it.

One solution for that is the London, which we've already seen.

In Chapter 3, we'll take a look at another one, which is the Trompowsky, characterized by White developing their bishop to g5 on move 2.

r1b1kb1r/1p1npppp/1p3n2/3p2B1/2pP4/2P1P3.text:
And we will support ours with ...Nbd7.

Moves like ...e6 and ...b5 are coming, with a healthy pawn chain and potential for expansion.

Our dark-squared bishop will be open and we don't have to worry about our c8-bishop yet.

Its time will come.

r3kb1r/pp2p2p/1qn2p2/3p1bp1/2pPn3/2P1P1B.text:
Let's develop instead and look to trap the bishop with ...h5 and ...h4.

Our king is safe in the center for now and we keep our options open for castling long if needed.

Black is on the verge of being winning.

rn2kb1r/pp2p2p/1q3p2/3p1bp1/2pPn3/2P1P1B.text:
Now the bishop has to retreat to g3.

We didn't force it there to capture it, however.

We only wanted to expand and we don't want to open up the h-file for them now.

rn2kb1r/pp2pp1p/1q6/3pBbp1/2pPn3/2P1P3/P.text:
White can move to the center before returning back to g3.

This provokes ...f6, but we're okay with that.

rn2kb1r/pp2pppp/1q6/3p1b2/2pPnB2/2P1P3/P.text:
White has to resort to even more passivity and retreat to c1.

But we're not done applying pressure.

Let's go after their bishop now!

rnb1kb1r/1p2pppp/1p3n2/3p2B1/2pP4/2P1P3/.text:
For now, let's finish development.

White activates their knight to d2.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/1Q3n2/3p2B1/2pP4/2P1P3/.text:
White takes on b6, which plays into our hands.

We'll recapture and now our rook is open, and we have prospects of pushing the b-pawn down the line.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/1q3n2/2pp2B1/3P4/1QP1P3.text:
White offers a trade of queens.

We don't want to capture and open up the a-file for them.

In fact, we would much prefer them to capture on b6.

Which is why ...c4 is a great move to ask the queen a question.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/1q3n2/3p2B1/2pP4/2P1P3/.text:
If White doesn't want to help us activate our pieces, they will retreat to c2 and continue defending the b2-pawn.

We'll get a bunch of activity and tempi in this line either way.

We'll jump to e4 in that case and attack the bishop.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/1q6/3p4/2pPnB2/2P1P3/PP.text:
There is another benefit to ...Ne4.

And that's to develop to f5 and threaten ...Ng3 with a discovered attack on the queen.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/1q6/3p4/3Pn2B/5N2/PPP2P.text:
The queen pressures the b2-pawn, and White can't retreat the dark-squared bishop to defend.

Our next ideas include ...Nc6 and the odd ...e5, a pawn sacrifice where we follow up with ...Bc5 and ...Bf5 or ...Bg4.

rnbQkb1r/pp3p1p/4pp2/2P5/2p5/4P3/PP3PPP/.text:
We don't even mind a queen trade.

It means less chances for White to attack.

rnbk3r/pp3p1p/4pp2/2b5/2B5/4P3/PP3PPP/RN.text:
We'll take on c5, with an easy position.

Our ideas are ...Ke7 to improve the king and prepare for the endgame, ...Nc6 to develop the knight to the best square and ...Bd7.

Our rooks will be connected and ready to join the game in the long run.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/5p2/2Pp4/8/4P3/PPP2PPP/.text:
Which they do.

Going for ...e5 now could be too dangerous as White would have the strong Qf3.

So I suggest the more solid ...e6, protecting the center and attacking the c5-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5B2/2pp4/3P4/4P3/PPP2PP.text:
White captures on f6 now 10% of the time.

We'll capture with the g-pawn as we did in Study 1.

However, the difference here is that we haven't played ...e5 yet so White can capture on c5.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2pp2B1/3P4/2P1P3/PP.text:
White plays c3 almost half the time here, as they want to reinforce the center.

However, there is something else we can take advantage of, and that's the b2-pawn being vulnerable.

When White moves the dark-squared bishop away early and we play ...c5, this is a common idea for Black.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2pp2B1/3P4/4PN2/PPP.text:
4.Nf3 is flexible and calm, allowing us to move forward with our plans.

It's played 11% of the time.

We'll jump to the center and attack the bishop first.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/8/2pp4/3Pn2B/4PN2/PPP2P.text:
Once it retreats to h4...

We can capture in the center once.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/8/3p4/3Pn2B/5N2/PPP2PPP.text:
Our point was to force the bishop to h4 first and then relieve the tension in the center.

So that we can attack some weaknesses unbothered.

rnbqkb1r/pp3p1p/4pp2/2Pp4/2P5/4P3/PP3PPP.text:
Don't be afraid of c4.

White does undermine our center, but we can always choose to simplify.

It's better to capture on c4 and keep our pawns together than allow White to capture and isolate them.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p2B1/3P4/4P3/PPP2.text:
3.e3 is played 25% of the time, in almost a million games. White connects the pawns and opens up the light-squared bishop.

One thing to keep in mind for us is that when White keeps the bishop on g5, ...Ne4 is a good response to attack it at a certain point.

But we'll go ...c5 for now. Don't go ...e6 and pin your own knight while blocking your bishop.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/6B1/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP.text:
The Trompowsky.

Let's expand in the center.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Study 2 will focus on White choosing to play e3 on move 3 rather than Bxf6.

In an unconventional Trompowsky approach, White claims their bishop on g5 is better and more active than our knight on f6 and wants to keep it there.

Let's begin.

lessons.title: White Plays d4, e3, c3 and f4

2rq1rk1/pp2nppp/3b4/2ppNp2/3PnP2/2P1P2R/.text:
By retreating the knight to e7 we don't allow White to trade it off, but instead, we'll kick away their knight with ...f6 on the next move. 

The knight could also guard our king in case White starts to attack.

2rq1rk1/pp3ppp/2nb1n2/2ppNp2/3P1P2/2P1PQ.text: White begins to shift the queen to the kingside.

2rq1rk1/pp3ppp/2nb1n2/2ppNp2/3P1P2/2P1PR.text:
White tries to bring more attackers to the kingside.

But we have a solid grip over the light-squares and by centralizing the knight to e4 we prepare to kick away White's knight from e5 by pushing ...f6.

White doesn't have this luxury since they've already pushed f4.

2rq1rk1/pp3ppp/2nb4/2ppNp2/3PnP2/2P1P2R/.text: White slides the rook to h3.

2rq1rk1/pp3ppp/2nbpn2/3p4/3P1P2/P2QPN1P/.text:
But our idea prevails after ...Rc8.

We'll play on the queenside with moves like ...Qb6 and ...Na5, while White's attack on the kingside isn't promising.

2rqr1k1/pp3ppp/2nb1n2/2ppNp2/3P1P2/2P1PQ.text:
The same plan applies also here:

We should centralize with ...Ne4, retreat the knight to e7 and kick away White's knight with ...f6.

Against the Stonewall where White's key idea is to keep the knight on e5, we simply have to commit to ...f6 at some point.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/2pp4/3P1P2/2PBP3/.text:
White has achieved their Stonewall structure.

Looks difficult to crack, but on the other hand our minor pieces have much more freedom.

Now we get to develop the bishop with tempo.

r2q1rk1/pp3pp1/2nbp2p/2pp1b2/3PnP1Q/2P1P.text:
But we respond with the knight's centralization and a queen trade offer.

After the queens are off, the attack will be non-existent and we'll enjoy great piece placement and play on the queenside regarding the c-file.

r2q1rk1/pp3pp1/2nbpn1p/2pp1b2/3P1P1Q/2P1.text: White could perhaps push g4 in the future.

r2q1rk1/pp3ppp/2nb1n2/2ppNp2/3P1P2/2P1P2.text:
White centralizes their knight.

But c8 is a great square for the rook, eyeing the c-file.

r2q1rk1/pp3ppp/2nb1n2/2ppNp2/3P1P2/2P1P3.text:
White finally starts to develop their queenside.

With ...Rc8 we can have future ideas of playing on the c-file with trading on d4.

This move is simply a must.

r2q1rk1/pp3ppp/2nbpn2/2pp1B2/3P1P2/2P1PN.text:
White trades as retreating would only benefit us.

We recapture and grip the e4-square.

r2q1rk1/pp3ppp/2nbpn2/2pp1b2/3P1P1Q/2P1P.text:
White tries to preserve their light-squared attacker.

But ...h6 guards the g5-square and prevents any Ng5 ideas.

r2q1rk1/pp3ppp/2nbpn2/2pp4/3P1Pb1/2PBPN1.text:
White kicks our our bishop.

...Bf5 to trade off the bishop should be played here.

This is a good general idea once your bishop is attacked on g4.

r2q1rk1/pp3ppp/2nbpn2/2pp4/3P1PbQ/2PBPN2.text:
White immediately brings the queen to the kingside.

It's important that we guard the h7-square by offering to trade the bishops.

r2q1rk1/pp3ppp/2nbpn2/2ppN3/3P1Pb1/2PBP3.text:
White has a strong grip on the e5-square, so they occupy it with the knight, which is one of their ideas in the Stonewall.

White's light-squared bishop is a strong attacker, so trading it off is a good idea here.

r2q1rk1/pp3ppp/2nbpn2/2ppNB2/3P1P2/2P1P3.text:
White doesn't give us the diagonal by retreating and trades instead.

We'll recapture with a strong grip over the e4-square.

These are the important dynamics one must know in positions like this one. 

Instead of trading our bishop for White's knight, we trade it for their bishop!

r2qk2r/pp3ppp/2nbpn2/2pp1b2/3P1P2/2PBPN1.text:
White creates a battery.

By trading on d4 we open up the c-file for our rook to generate counterplay there.

We are simply playing around White's structure and trying to take advantage of any weak points.

r2qk2r/pp3ppp/2nbpn2/2pp4/3P1Pb1/2PBPN1P.text:
White asks our bishop a question.

We'll answer with ...Bf5, aiming to trade off White's strong attacker.

r2qk2r/pp3ppp/2nbpn2/2pp4/3P1Pb1/2PBPN2/.text:
White could develop here instead.

We'll get the king to safety.

White shifts their queen to e1, aiming to join the attack on the kingside.

We can safely castle here.

Our minor pieces will do a good job defending the king.

r2qk2r/pp3ppp/2nbpn2/3p1b2/3P1P2/3BPN1P/.text:
White couldn't recapture with the e-pawn since the f4-pawn would hang.

Now we trade, this was our goal.

r2qk2r/pp3ppp/2nbpn2/3p4/3P1P2/3QPN1P/PP.text:
White recaptures.

We'll get the king to safety.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/2pp4/3P1Pb1/2PBPN2.text:
White blocks the attack by bringing the knight out.

Our light-squared bishop is already developed so we can push ...e6 without any worry.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2pp4/3P1Pb1/2PBPN2.text:
White waits with castling and starts to develop their queenside instead.

We bring out the bishop to its usual square in the Stonewall.

White gets castled.

We bring out the bishop to d6 and look over the e5-square.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/5n2/p1Ppp3/1P6/2PBP3/P4P.text:
White solidifies the b4-pawn.

We'll trade.

rnbqkb1r/5ppp/1p3n2/2Ppp3/1P6/3BP3/P4PPP.text:
And we'll try to chip away at the c5-pawn yet again and enjoy the semi-open a-file for our rook.

We should eventually come out on top and shatter White's pawn structure.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2Pp4/8/3BP3/PPP2PPP.text:
White could grab the pawn on c5.

This obviously isn't the Stonewall anymore, but still we should know what to do.

It's very rare, played 7% of the time.

In the absence of the d4-pawn, we can freely grab the center with ...e5!

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2pp4/3P4/2PBP3/PP3P.text:
White solidifies their center with c3, which is played 70% of the game.

Now that we've pushed ...c5, it's time to develop the knight.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/5n2/2Ppp3/1P6/3BP3/P1P2P.text:
White tries to hold onto the c5-pawn.

We try to chip away at White's queenside structure by pushing ...a5.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/3P4/3BP3/PPP2P.text:
White brings out the light-squared bishop, as they do in 20% of the games.

Nf3 would block their f-pawn, so now we can be pretty sure that they'll go for the Stonewall with f4.

We wait with the b8-knight's development and put some pressure on White's central d4-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/3P4/4P3/PPP2PPP/.text:
White plays e3, going for the solid Stonewall setup with c3 and f4.

The big downside of this approach is that their bishop on c1 will be stuck behind their pawn structure.

Now it is time to push ...d5, opening up the light-squared bishop and controlling the central e4- and c4-squares.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Let's analyze how to face the Stonewall setup as Black now.

The setup got its name for its very solid appearance which looks hard to crack.

That means it's extremely important for Black to stay active.

lessons.title: White Plays d4, e3 and Nf3

r2q1rk1/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/7b/1b1PN3/3B1N1P/P.text: White blocks the attack with their bishop.

r2q1rk1/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/7b/3PN3/3B1N1P/PP1.text:
And suddenly after a trade on d2, White's center is collapsing due to the pin on the f3-knight.

Pushing in the center doesn't always pay off!

r2q1rk1/pp3ppp/2nbpn2/2pp3b/3PP3/2PB1N1P.text:
This is the most popular, yet a bad plan. 

Our pieces have a lot of activity.

Let's see how we can punish this move. First we trade, isolating the d4-pawn.

r2q1rk1/pp3ppp/2nbpn2/3p3b/3PP3/3B1N1P/P.text:
White recaptures.

We'll trade in the center yet again.

r2q1rk1/pp3ppp/2nbpn2/7b/3PN3/3B1N1P/PP3.text:
White recaptures.

We'll save the bishop pair for now and attack White's rook.

r2q1rk1/ppbn1ppp/2p1pn2/2Pp3b/PP1P4/2N1P.text:
White continues to expand.

...Re8 further prepares ...e5.

It becomes pretty clear why ...e5 is our main idea.

r2qk2r/pp1n1ppp/2pbpn2/2Pp3b/3P4/2N1PN1P.text:
White sees the opportunity to gain space with tempo by pushing c5 and play on the queenside with b4 and a4 next.

It's important that we retreat to c7 and keep guarding the e5-square, so that we'll be able to push ...e5 in the next few moves.

r2qk2r/pp3ppp/2nbpn2/2pp3b/3P4/2PBPN1P/P.text:
In The Colle System, White slowly prepares to push e4.

Let's just castle the king and get it out of the center.

r2qk2r/pp3ppp/2nbpn2/2pp4/3P2b1/2PBPN1P/.text:
White kicks out our bishop.

We'll keep the pin by retreating to h5.

r2qk2r/ppbn1ppp/2p1pn2/2Pp3b/1P1P4/2N1PN.text:
White continues to grab space on the queenside.

Committing to this queenside approach and closing down their central role is risky for White, as it gives us all the central control in terms of pawn breaks.

Before initiating any action in the center, we should hide the king.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/2pp4/3P2b1/2PBPN2/.text:
White develops the knight as well.

But ...e6 adds some support to the d5-pawn and opens up our dark-squared bishop.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2pp4/3P2b1/2PBPN2/.text:
White gets their king to safety.

We'll develop the bishop to d6 as Black should do in these structures without White's dark-squared bishop developed.

r2qr1k1/ppbn1ppp/2p1pn2/1PPp3b/P2P4/2N1P.text: Our opponent plays on the queenside with b5 and tries to attack our pawn chain...

r2qr1k1/ppbn1ppp/2p2n2/1PPpp2b/P2P4/2N1P.text:
But a good answer to a flank attack is to create action in the center!

Black has a comfortable position with all of their pieces playing.

There might be some trades incoming in case White captures on e5 with the knight, but we don't mind them.

If not, we can consider pushing ...e4.

rn1qk2r/pp3ppp/2pbpn2/3p3b/2PP4/2N1PN1P/.text:
White starts to develop the queenside pieces.

We do as well.

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/3bpn2/3p3b/2PP4/4PN1P/PP.text:
White puts pressure on our central pawn.

We'll reinforce it with ...c6.

Pretty logical so far.

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/3bpn2/3p4/3P2b1/4PN1P/PP.text:
White attacks our bishop.

We'll retreat to h5 and keep its diagonal.

rn1qkb1r/pp1n1pp1/2p1p1p1/3p4/2PP2P1/4P2.text:
By pushing ...c6 we support the d5-pawn and block the view of the bishop on g2.

Now if White plays Nc3, we can actually grab on c4 and defend it with ...Nb6.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2pp4/3P2b1/2PBPN2/P.text:
White supports the d-pawn with c3.

Now it's the right time to develop the knight to its natural square.

This position is The London but with the exception that White's bishop is stuck on c1!

rn1qkb1r/ppp1ppp1/6b1/3pP2p/6PP/4P3/PPP2.text:
And after ...h5 we get to keep our bishop pair and aim at White's overextended kingside pawns which could prove to be a weakness in the future.

We've untangled ourselves out of this situation.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p3b/3P2P1/4PN1P/P.text:
White attacks further with g4 to break the pin.

We simply retreat to g6.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/3P2b1/3BPN2/PP.text:
The second most popular move occurs in 16% of the games, as White develops the bishop to d3 and controls the e4-square.

We'll put some pressure on the d4-pawn with ...c5 before bringing out the knight to c6.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/3P2b1/4PN1P/PP.text:
In 11% of the games White immediately kicks out our bishop from g4.

We should always retreat to h5.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/3P2b1/4PN2/PPP.text:
35% of the time White breaks the pin with Be2 and prepares to castle.

We support the d5-pawn and open up the dark-squared bishop.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5nb1/3pN3/3P2P1/4P2P/P.text:
White goes after our light-squared bishop, since it's a pretty good piece.

This is the most active plan; we keep the knight on b8 in reserve and challenge White's e5-knight.

...Nbd7 would allow h4 as White and suddenly Black's position is very passive.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/3P2b1/4PN2/PPP.text:
White hides their king.

We'll bring the bishop to d6 to cover the e5-square and prepare to push ...e5 in the future.

rn1qkb1r/pppn1pp1/4p1p1/3p4/2PP2P1/4P2P/.text: White challenges the d5-pawn which plays in with their fianchettoed bishop on g2.

rn1qkb1r/pppnppp1/6p1/3p4/3P2P1/4P2P/PPP.text:
White fianchettoes.

We will play ...e6 to support the d5-pawn and open up our light-squared bishop.

rn1qkb1r/pppnpppp/6N1/3p4/3P2P1/4P2P/PPP.text:
White gets rid of our light-squared bishop.

We recapture with the h-pawn, of course, opening up the rook.

rn1qkb1r/pppnpppp/6b1/3pN3/3P2PP/4P3/PPP.text:
White tries to trap our bishop with h4, aiming for h5.

Let's trade off the knight first.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/3P4/4PN2/PPP2P.text:
With e3, our opponent goes for the Colle system, aiming to quickly bring out the light-squared bishop to d3 and push for e4.

After the London, it is the second most popular move with 21% occurrence.

White doesn't have the luxury of developing their queenside bishop, but we do, and we'll pin the knight.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/3P4/5N2/PPP1PPPP.text:
White brings out their knight as well, keeping their setup secret for now.

We'll also place a pawn in the center.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In Chapter 5, White adapts the so called "Colle System". 

It's similar to the Stonewall, but White brings out the knight to f3 and slowly aims to push e4.

Let's check out how we should approach this setup!

r2q1rk1/ppp1ppbp/2n2np1/8/2BP2bQ/2N1BN2/.text:
White defends the pawn on d4. 

The fact that they're busy defending is a good sign: we've neutralized the gambit.

10...e6 makes our f7-pawn safer, and we also get the e7-square to maneuver.

r2q1rk1/ppp2pbp/2n1pnp1/4N3/2BP2bQ/2N1B3.text:
11.Ng5 h6 is winning for us. White does not have an attack.

11.Ne5 attacks our bishop on g4.

r2q1rk1/ppp2pbp/2n1pnp1/4Nb2/2BP3Q/2N1B3.text:
But we can simply go to f5. 

12.g4 does not work. 12...Nxg4 is the right response because the queen on h4 is not protected. 

Our plan is to trade more pieces and convert our material advantage.

r2qk2r/pQpbbppp/2n2p2/8/3Pp3/2N5/PPP2PPP.text:
But the pawn on b7 isn't as valuable as a center pawn. 

We're attacking d4 and ...Rb1 is coming. 

White won't be able to defend against all the threats and Black is winning.

r2qkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pnb1/6B1/2BP4/2N2N2/.text:
But we block the c4-bishop and get ready to play ...Be7 to castle and defend our king. 

We've made sure to play things safe, which is exactly what we must do. 

Now it's a matter of playing up a pawn.

r2qkb1r/pp1npppp/2p2n2/5bB1/3Pp3/2N2P2/P.text:
White offers a pawn to get rid of our e4-pawn.

We will accept it at this point.

r2qkb1r/pp1npppp/2p2n2/6B1/2BPb3/2N2N2/P.text:
White develops their bishop, putting pressure on f7.

We fall back and defend it.

r2qkb1r/pp1npppp/2p2nb1/6B1/2BP4/2N2N2/P.text: White castles, with a powerful rook coming into the game.

r2qkb1r/pppnpppp/5n2/5bB1/3PP3/2N5/PPP3P.text:
White trades.

We capture on e4. 

7.Nxe4 Nxe4 gives us a centralized knight with a tempo on the bishop on g5.

r2qkb1r/pppnpppp/5n2/6B1/3Pb3/2N2N2/PPP3.text:
White develops their other knight to f3.

We cover the b5- and d5-squares.

A bit of consolidation once we've secured the extra pawn.

r3kb1r/pp1npppp/2p2n2/q4bB1/3P4/2N2N2/PP.text:
And we develop our queen to a5. 

We will consolidate with ...e6, ...h6, ...Bb4 and ...Bh7. 

White has a tough road ahead if they want to prove compensation.

r4rk1/ppp1ppbp/2nq1np1/6B1/2BP2b1/2N2N2/.text:
We have an idea: ...Bxf3 and ...Rad8 to put pressure on d4. 

White could play 11.Nb5, but we have 11...Qd7. 

Our middlegame plan is to continue attacking d4 and to trade pieces whenever possible.

rn1q1rk1/ppp1ppbp/5np1/6B1/2BP2b1/2N2N2/.text:
White creates a queen and bishop battery.

We have an attack on d4.

rn1q1rk1/ppp1ppbp/5np1/8/2BP2bQ/2N2N2/PP.text:
The queen indirectly guards d4.

White prepares the idea of Ng5 to put pressure on h7.

We here add another attacker on d4. The good thing is that Ng5 does not work because it drops d4 with a fork.

rn1qk2r/pQpbbppp/5p2/8/3Pp3/2N5/PPP2PPP/.text: White takes on b7, winning a pawn back.

rn1qk2r/ppp1bppp/5p2/1Q3b2/3Pp3/2N5/PPP2.text:
Check!

We have to block with our bishop.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/5bB1/3Pp3/2N5/PPP.text:
White castles.

We develop the queenside knight and support the one on f6. 

White cannot win the pawn.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5B2/5b2/3Pp3/2N5/PPP2P.text:
This is the most common move. 

The idea is to double our pawns and undermine the defense of e4.

We'll recapture away from the center so that our f8-bishop can come into play.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/5bB1/3Pp3/2N2P2/PP.text:
White loses all hopes of capturing on e4.

Instead, they offer up the f-pawn trade to make us voluntarily clear the center.

Since we have two pieces defending e4, we can simply develop.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/5bB1/3Pp3/2N5/PPP1.text:
White attacks the e4-pawn. 

Again, we don't want to take d4 because of Qb5+ ideas.

So, we prevent Qb5+.

If 6.Bxf6, we're happy to see that move because we get the bishop pair.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/5p2/5b2/3Pp3/2N5/PPP1QP.text:
White attacks e4 and leaves d4 hanging. 

We don't want to go pawn hunting, as Qb5+ causes more problems if our queen isn't on d8.

Instead, we want to develop.

rn1qkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3pPb2/3P4/2N2N2/PPP.text:
But we're easily consolidating. 

A simple but effective plan against this Nc3 setup is ...Nc6 and ...Nb4 to attack c2.

rnb1k2r/ppp2ppp/3bp3/5q2/8/2N1QN2/PPP3PP.text:
Converting this game should be easy. 

We will develop with moves like ...Nc6 and ...O-O. We have a massive threat of ...Bf4. 

If 12.Nd5, 12...h5 helps us prevent 13.g4, since White might want g4 and Rg1.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/5q2/8/2N1BN2/PPP2Q.text:
The knight is developed. 

They block the queen trade, but we can trade something else.

This is a fork. We will trade our knight for the bishop.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/8/3q4/2N1BQ2/PPP3P.text:
White develops with a tempo, but fortunately we can move away with a tempo as well.

Offering queen trades gives us tempi because White does not want to trade queens down material. 

7.O-O-O is popular, but we can simply trade queens.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/8/6q1/2N1B3/PPP2QP.text:
White avoids the trade.

We offer the trade once more.

We should annoy White as much as we can.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1pppp/8/5q2/6n1/2N1BN2/PPP1Q.text:
The queen moves away.

We trade. 

This is exactly what we want because we are up material.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1pppp/8/5q2/8/2N1QN2/PPP3PP/.text:
White recaptures. 

Let us briefly evaluate the position. 

We are up two pawns and have the bishop pair. I rest my case.

We play 10...e6 to develop our dark-squared bishop.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/5np1/6B1/2BP4/2N2N2/PP.text:
White attacks our knight. 

Because we have a pawn on e7, this move is not effective.

8...Bg4, on the other hand, does pin the knight on f3. 

We undermine the defense of d4 and threaten to exchange pieces.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/5np1/8/2BP4/2N2N2/PPP3.text:
The queen goes to e1. 

The idea is to transfer to h4 and attack our kingside.

Our idea is to undermine d4. 

The threat is ...Bxf3 and ...Qxd4+, winning the bishop on c4.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/5np1/8/2BP4/2N2N2/PPP3P.text:
White castles. 

Here, a benefit of 4.f3 is unveiled: their rook becomes active on the f-file.

Castling helps us add another defender to f7.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/5np1/8/2BP4/2N2N2/PPP3.text:
The next best square for White's bishop is c4. 

It puts pressure on f7.

We fianchetto.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3p4/3PP3/2N5/PPP2P.text:
But if White plays 3.e4 anyways, this leads to the Blackmar-Diemer Gambit.

3.e4 is played about 10% of the time.

We'll of course take. This is already slightly better for Black if played correctly.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3pP3/3P4/8/PPP1BP1.text:
Our knight is attacked and forced to a worse square.

But these positions are only good for White if they have a concrete line to gain an advantage. 

Their development of one piece is not enough compensation for them.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/6B1/3Pp3/2N5/PPP2P.text:
18% of games go like this. 

The purpose of 4.Bg5 is to undermine the defense of e4.

White wants to develop while trying to get back the pawn.

We can develop and defend e4.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/8/3P4/2N2N2/PPP3PP.text:
5.Nxf3 is the most popular recapture. 

The knight is a dangerous piece. It can jump to e5 or g5 and attack our f7-pawn.

I suggest 5...g6 here to fianchetto.

But another benefit of this move is that it blocks the h7-pawn so White won't be able to attack our kingside with Bd3.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/8/3P4/2N2Q2/PPP3PP.text:
5.Qxf3 is nearly -2 according to the engine. 

It instantly puts pressure on b7. But the queen defended something important...

That's two pawns, which is why the engine gave this position a -2 evaluation in our favor.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/8/3Pp3/2N2P2/PPP3P.text:
60% of games continue like this. 

White offers a second pawn for quicker development and to get rid of our important e4-pawn.

Even though White gets some activity, there are clever ways to defend and keep a safe position, so we'll take.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3PP1n1/8/PPP1BP1.text:
If they develop and attack, we must retreat.

We here attack e4. 

The move e5 isn't that big of a threat because White lacks a follow-up.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/3P2P1/8/PPP1PP1P.text:
This is technically called the Gibbins-Weidenhagen Gambit, but you don't need to remember such a lofty name for this opening. 

The important thing is that it's less than 1% of games, and Black gets a small advantage.

White wants to give up the g4-pawn to get strong central control.

We'll take.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/3P4/2N5/PPP1PPPP.text:
This looks like White could go for a Jobava London.

We play d5 and establish central presence. 

This makes moves like e4 harder to play...

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/8/8/3PP1n1/8/PPP2P1P/R.text:
White wants to occupy the center and attack our knight.

But we can challenge their center and defend our knight with 3...d5.

This variation already nearly refutes their gambit. 

4.e5 Bf5 is good for us.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3pP3/3P4/2N5/PPP1BP1.text:
White develops and puts pressure on d5.

But because their pawns are on d4 and e5, we get the f5-square for our bishop like in the advanced Caro-Kann.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text: For this last chapter, I want to teach you some sound lines against two White Gambits: The Blackmar-Diemer and the 2.g4 gambit.
